REUTERS/Toby Melville If arriving by train, alight at St Leonards Warrior Square station and walk down Kings Road, a vibrant street of cafes, second-hand bookshops, vintage furniture stores and artist-run outlets selling bold screenprints and ceramics. It holds a street market on the first Saturday of each month, featuring handicrafts, organic food, and jewellery. Turn left at the end of the road for your first glimpse of the sea. What to see: One of my favourite spots on the beach is the strip along Warrior Square and Bottle Alley, a split-level promenade. Beachfront cafes such as Goat Ledge , Starsky & Hatch and The Selkie have breathed new life into this area, and it is a popular place to bask in the sun with a coffee or lunch. The brightly painted wooden huts, twinkly lights and bistro tables on the pebbles bring a festival vibe and you’ll often hear live music here. A short walk further along the seafront brings you to George Street, a charming pedestrian lane of restaurants, pubs and gift shops at the foot of the castle. The West Hill lift is a historic Victorian funicular railway that will transport you up to the Norman castle for £5.50 ($7.40) round-trip. There you’ll find magnificent views across the English Channel towards France, as well as yoga classes and outdoor film screenings. The West Hill is also home to the Smugglers Adventure , a fun attraction that tells stories of piracy and smuggling in a warren of caves reputedly once used to conceal contraband. In the 1960s, the caves housed a subterranean nightclub. To return to the Old Town, hop back on the funicular or follow one of the several steep, winding paths. Look out for the twittens — narrow, medieval alleyways between the houses, as you weave through All Saints Street, Tackleway and the High Street. What to eat: If you fancy seafood, the grilled “catch of the day” fish bap (or sandwich) at Goat Ledge is always delicious. Alternatively, pick up traditional fish and chips and eat them on the beach. Just watch out for diving seagulls going for your chips. People relax at Goat Ledge beach cafe at St Leonards-on-Sea. REUTERS/Toby Melville People relax at Selkie Seafood Bar at St Leonards-on-Sea. REUTERS/Toby Melville Oyster shells and other sea food are seen on a beachside table at Selkie Seafood Bar at St Leonards-on-Sea. REUTERS/Toby Melville In St Leonards, Half Man! Half Burger! has some of the best burgers — meat and vegetarian — I've ever tasted, and Three Faces has incredible tapas. Culture fix: Hastings is unusual in having a beach-launched fishing fleet, with the boats hauled back on to the pebbles when not in use. Right beside them is Hastings Contemporary , a wonderful art gallery whose design mirrors that of the historic black Net Shops used for stowing fishing equipment. A fisherman throws equipment from a boat after returning from a fishing trip in The Stade area of Hastings Old Town. Hastings has one of the largest working beach-launched fishing fleets in Europe. REUTERS/Toby Melville A tractor pulls a fishing boat up the beach in The Stade area of Hastings Old Town. REUTERS/Toby Melville Walk along Rock-a-Nore Road and stop at the excellent (and free) Fishermen's Museum , which highlights the history of the fleet and tragic storms that have struck. Opposite is the 1902 East Hill lift, Britain's steepest funicular, which takes you up to Hastings Country Park — a beautiful expanse of rolling sandstone cliffs, with breathtaking views down to the sea. Look out for the roaming ponies that graze the heathland. A young person views exhibits at the Fishermen's Museum in Hastings Old Town. REUTERS/Toby Melville For music lovers, Hastings Philharmonic runs excellent classical concerts throughout the year. Check the tides: Hastings has a pebble beach, but at low tide, vast stretches of sand are exposed, offering ample space for long strolls. I like to time sea swims for high tide and beach walks for low tide. If this falls at sunset, you'll find the beach packed with locals savouring the views. Look out for hagstones, pebbles with natural holes. A few times a year, when the tide falls below 60 cm (2 feet), you can glimpse the wreck of the Amsterdam, a Dutch East India Company ship that ran aground in 1749 outside St Leonards and was exposed by shifting sands in 1969. It makes for an eerie sight. A replica is moored outside Amsterdam's Maritime Museum , while Hastings' excellent Shipwreck Museum displays the bottles, spoons and other goods found onboard. The 1066 battlefield: A 15-minute train ride 6 miles (9.5 km) inland brings you to the town of Battle, where King Harold’s Saxon army was defeated by William’s Norman invaders. You can visit the former battlefield and ruined abbey, built by William's son on the spot where Harold perished, and explore a medieval gatehouse. Centuries on, walking the trail around the battlefield where thousands died remains a sombre and moving experience. A good pint: Hastings has no shortage of charming local boozers. The 16th-century Stag Inn on All Saints Street has a pretty, tiered garden overlooking the rooftops. Look out for the mummified cat that was found encased within the chimney — a practice said to ward off evil in British folklore. Another good pub is the FILO (First In Last Out) on the High Street, with an unusual indoor fire pit and cosy wooden booths that are always packed on weekends. It brews its own traditional ales and has been joined in recent years by other craft beer makers, including The Brewing Brothers , who run three excellent venues. In the Old Town, the Jenny Lind , named after a 19th-century Swedish opera singer, is one of Hastings' most-loved pubs with regular acoustic nights and folk, rock and sea shanty sessions. Over in St Leonards, The Piper draws a younger crowd and holds regular gigs upstairs. Get festive: Dig out green clothes and flower crowns for the annual "Jack in the Green" folk festival on the first Monday of May. Dancers and drummers dressed in green parade through the town and up on to the West Hill, where the Jack — a crowned figure clad in foliage — is symbolically slain to release the spirit of summer. It's all rather reminiscent of the 1973 folk horror film "The Wicker Man," and seems to get bigger every year. A participant attends the annual May Day bank holiday Jack In The Green parade and festival. REUTERS/Toby Melville Participants attend the annual May Day bank holiday Jack In The Green parade and festival. REUTERS/Toby Melville A participant attends the annual May Day bank holiday Jack In The Green parade and festival. REUTERS/Toby Melville In July, locals rustle up striped shirts and eye patches for Pirate Weekend , which brings three days of live music to the shore, and a noisy parade through the town for all “pirates” to join. In October, an annual bonfire marks the anniversary of the Norman Conquest, with a flaming torch procession through the Old Town and a huge blaze and fireworks on the beach. CITY MEMO DATA POINTS Population: 91,000 Price of a cup of coffee: £3.80 ($5) for a flat white at Starsky & Hatch Price of an ice cream: £3.00 ($4) for a Flake 99 — vanilla soft-serve served in a wafer cone with a small chocolate bar on top — from Dom's Ices . For £3.90 ($5.17), you can get a scoop of gelato at Di Pola's . Great place to see a sunset: The coastal paths of the Country Park, or the West or East Hill

item.title: Record-breaking Renshaw puts Australia on top in Durban
item.description: Matt Renshaw struck a career-best 190 to guide Australia to 390 all out on day two of the first test against South Africa at Kingsmead on Saturday, as the home side reached 27 for one in reply before play was ended prematurely by bad light.
item.dc:creator: Mark Gleeson
item.content:encoded: Matt Renshaw struck a career-best 190 to guide Australia to 390 all out on day two of the first test against South Africa at Kingsmead on Saturday, as the home side reached 27 for one in reply before play was ended prematurely by bad light. Aiden Markram (15 not out) and David Bedingham (12 not out) will resume on the third morning for South Africa, who were frustrated by the record-breaking innings of Renshaw. Ryan Rickelton was the hosts' wicket to fall when he was caught at third slip by Beau Webster for a duck off the bowling of Josh Hazlewood. The day belonged to Renshaw as he shared a record ninth-wicket stand of 134 for Australia against South Africa with Nathan Lyon (27), also the highest partnership for that wicket in Durban. "There was a lot of thinking today while batting," Renshaw said. "How many balls can I face? How do I get off strike when I need to? It was thinking what we can try and do, trying to find the right options, find a boundary if we could. "Keeping them out in the field, getting their quicks coming back on. I saw (Marco) Jansen bowled 30-odd (overs), (Anrich) Nortje 30-odd, so they've got some overs into the frontline bowlers in the first innings of the first game." His score is the highest by a number five batter in tests at Kingsmead, but he was out soon after tea when he edged spinner Simon Harmer to Markram at slip. Australia were in trouble early in Renshaw's innings as they slipped to 124 for six on day one. EARLY TROUBLE But Renshaw flipped the script after putting on 86 for the seventh wicket with skipper Pat Cummins (43). Australia started the second day on 187 for six and frustrated the home side before Wiaan Mulder (4-68) had Cummins caught by Markram at second slip. Mitchell Starc (6) followed quickly after being bowled by Mulder, and at it looked as though South Africa would run through the lower order. Lyon was circumspect, however, and Renshaw rotated the strike superbly to make sure he had most of the strike and continued to accumulate runs rather than attack the bowling. Lyon fell LBW to Marco Jansen (3-68). Renshaw’s 190 has come off 397 balls, a classic test innings of patience and waiting for the bad ball. He was struck in the helmet by speedster Anrich Nortje, but he soon settled again and his second test century came nine years after his first, 185 against Pakistan in 2017. Renshaw had made single-figure scores in 11 of his previous 13 test innings. "He played beautifully throughout the innings, played what was in front of him and left well," Mulder said. "The partnerships built around him and he played the situation as well as anyone could have at this level. "It is a good cricket wicket and will get a bit up and down as the game goes on and spin more."

item.title: Rosatom and Finland's Fennovoima claim different wins after tribunal ruling
item.description: Russia's state nuclear corporation Rosatom and Finnish utility Fennovoima each highlighted different parts of an International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) tribunal ruling as favourable on Saturday, in a long-running dispute over the cancelled Hanhikivi-1 nuclear power project.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Russia's state nuclear corporation Rosatom and Finnish utility Fennovoima each highlighted different parts of an International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) tribunal ruling as favourable on Saturday, in a long-running dispute over the cancelled Hanhikivi-1 nuclear power project. The parties have been locked in legal disputes since Fennovoima scrapped the 7-billion-euro ($7.8 billion) project in May 2022, citing significant delays and political risks shortly after Russia launched its conflict in Ukraine . Rosatom said the tribunal found that Fennovoima had unlawfully terminated the contract for the construction of the planned plant in northern Finland. "Today's victory is important, but not final. We will continue to prove that we are right regarding the Finnish project in courts of various instances," Rosatom Director General Alexey Likhachev said in a statement, which did not refer to any financial outcome. Fennovoima said the tribunal found that it had not been entitled to terminate the contract, but that it was entitled to receive reimbursements of advance payments and interest in excess of 1 billion euros ($1.12 billion). It said the tribunal offset both sides' claims, resulting in Rosatom subsidiaries being ordered to pay Fennovoima a net 606 million euros plus interest. The ICC did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The contract to build the 1.2 gigawatt plant was signed in 2013 with Fennovoima, a consortium in which Finnish stakeholders including Fortum, Outokumpu and SSAB originally controlled two thirds through a joint venture, and the Russian side held one third. After the project's termination, Fennovoima wound down its operations and is primarily engaged in legal proceedings. ($1 = 0.8928 euros)

item.title: Russian attack on Ukrainian city kills 20, a day after Trump eases diesel sanctions on Moscow
item.description: The strike on Zaporizhzhia, which killed three children, came a day after President Trump announced a deal to lift sanctions on Russian diesel.
item.dc:creator: Sergiy Chalyi, Max Hunder
item.content:encoded: Twenty people, including three children, were killed in a Russian attack on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia on Saturday, a day after US President Donald Trump announced a deal to lift sanctions on Russian diesel in a major setback for Kyiv. "Today, Russia said thank you for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said, in some of his sharpest criticism yet of the White House. Zaporizhzhia has been a regular target of Russian bombardment with strikes [USN:L8N43Z01W TEXT:"intensifying in the past few months."] A 6-year-old girl was among those killed when one strike reduced part of an apartment block to rubble. Her grandfather, Anatoliy Chumniy, stood sobbing over her body, laid on the ground in a white bag, after rescuers pulled it from the wreckage. "Her birthday would have been at the end of the month," he said through tears. Eighteen others were wounded in the attack on the industrial city, with a pre-war population of over 700,000 and whose outskirts lie less than 30 km (20 miles) from the front line. RUSSIA ESCALATING ATTACKS ON UKRAINIAN CITIES It was the third mass-casualty attack on Ukraine this week. Nearly 80 civilians were killed in Russian strikes on Wednesday and Thursday, including at least 30 killed by a bomb in the eastern garrison city of Kramatorsk and 22 others by a missile in the town of Pryluky, 80 miles east of Kyiv. A senior official in Zaporizhzhia, Mykhailo Semikin, said Russia had hit several locations simultaneously in the early hours of Saturday. Rescuers clambered through crumbled masonry to pull other residents of the building out alive. One man, whose leg was trapped in the rubble, screamed in pain as he was being freed. "If (the Russians) have money, they’ll be able to carry on fighting us," said Nataliia Malysheva, a 49-year-old local resident whose parents died in hospital after being pulled from the rubble. "How many lives have been lost here, how many homes have been destroyed? How many innocent people have died in the meantime?" MOSCOW NEEDS 'DIFFERENT SIGNALS' "Last night provided yet more confirmation that Russia perceives any easing of pressure as a signal that it can supposedly keep fighting, that it can supposedly keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed," Zelenskiy said. A missile attack on Saturday afternoon also hit a restaurant, wounding seven people in Kyiv. Russian drones flew over Kyiv throughout the day, part of a vast new wave of bombardment of the capital, the heaviest since the early days of the war. Russia’s Defence Ministry said on Saturday its drones had struck a data-processing centre in Kyiv and a cargo ship carrying military supplies to the Ukrainian port of Odesa. TRUMP LIFTS DIESEL SANCTIONS Trump's decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports comes as his administration seeks to curb fuel prices, which have risen sharply during the US conflict with Iran . Kyiv had instead urged Washington to increase pressure on Moscow in an effort to force it into serious negotiations to end the four-and-a-half-year war . Trump, meanwhile, has criticised Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, which he claims have driven up global prices. Kyiv has said it wants a total halt on all energy strikes by both sides as Moscow pummels Ukraine's power grid. On Saturday, parts of Kyiv and the surrounding region were left without power, bringing the city's metro trains to a complete halt for the second time this week. The latest strikes came after Ukrainian and European officials held talks with US negotiators in Miami on Friday aimed at developing a common proposal for ending the war, according to [USN:FWN45V1JO TEXT:"a person familiar with the discussions"]. Trump announced the diesel deal while the negotiations were underway, a move Zelenskiy said had caught Kyiv by surprise. The Ukrainian delegation was headed home on Saturday, presidential aide Dmytro Lytvyn was cited by the Interfax Ukraine news agency as saying. Russian President Vladimir Putin said after a call with Trump that an immediate resumption of peace talks was unlikely, citing Ukrainian drone attacks on Moscow. US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner may visit Moscow within the next two weeks, Russian state news agency TASS reported on Saturday, citing a source. Four civilians were killed and five others were wounded as a result of Ukrainian attacks on the [USN:S8N42201C TEXT:"Russian-controlled Luhansk region"] in eastern Ukraine, the Russian-installed governor said on Saturday. Reuters could not independently verify the report and there was no immediate comment from Ukraine.

item.title: Jocelyn Bioh on why Broadway is finally ready for 'School Girls'
item.description: The playwright and actor talks beauty, colorism, and how Broadway has changed in the decade since she wrote the play.
item.dc:creator: Kathryn Lurie
item.content:encoded:
Playwright Jocelyn Bioh during an interview with Reuters in New York City. REUTERS/Brendan McDermid Nearly a decade after Jocelyn Bioh wrote “School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play,” the play itself has barely changed. But the world around it has. The comedy about a group of teenage girls at a Ghanaian boarding school premiered off-Broadway in 2017, launching Bioh’s career as a playwright and going on to become a hit at regional theaters across the United States. But despite its success, Bioh was told it might not belong on Broadway. Now “School Girls” has made it there — following the Broadway success of Bioh’s “Jaja’s African Hair Braiding” in 2023 — and she is finding an audience that responds differently to the play’s exploration of body image, the privileging of lighter skin, known as colorism, and the often brutal social dynamics of girlhood. Beneath its rapid-fire jokes and teenage rivalries is a more painful story about who gets to be considered beautiful — and what people are willing to do to fit that ideal. Speaking in New York City, Bioh discusses what has changed since “School Girls” was first produced, the universality of teenage insecurity and why bringing the play to Broadway feels like coming full circle. This conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

How does it feel to finally bring “School Girls” to Broadway? It feels incredibly humbling. This play changed my life. It was the first play of mine that ever got produced. I can very clearly mark what my life was like before opening night of that show and then after. That audiences and critics all still feel the same way nearly a decade later is a reminder that I was on the right track. It also feels doubly exciting because even though it had so much success regionally and has been all over the country, I was told, “It's a great play, but maybe it's not the right fit for a Broadway stage.”

What do you think was meant by that, and what has changed enough for it to be on Broadway now? Broadway shows were very specific then. They didn't have ensembles that looked like the cast of “School Girls.” It was a lot of celebrities, a lot of things that seemed to fit into one specific category or box. The world has shifted. Audiences are different than they were 10 years ago. In a lot of ways, “Jaja's African Hair Braiding” having so much success was a marker that, a Broadway play is just a play that's on Broadway. It doesn't necessarily have to fit a specific category.

Is there anything in the play that hits differently than it did when you first wrote it? The conversation around beauty standards and body image has shifted in the last 10 years. Some would say (for the) better, some would say worse, but we're all aware of it in a different way. The play kicks off with Paulina bullying Nana about her size and her eating. You can feel the audience is immediately on Nana's side. Halfway through the play, she has a moment where she really stands up to Paulina, and every night that moment gets applause. You can feel the audience cheering, almost jumping up ready to fight with her. They're taking off their earrings! We did not have that experience off-Broadway. I think we were in a time where we accepted the idea that if you were somebody who was bigger, you should be losing weight; you should be trying to conform. Our ideas of beauty are very different now. Big ships turn slow, but I appreciate that I can feel that in the audience. Did you rewrite much for this production? Very small things, little jokes that I thought would land better. But the play is still largely the same thing I wrote in 2016. If I were sitting down to write this play now, I don't know that I would be as honest or as vulnerable as I was then, particularly in the moments where Paulina is speaking very directly about how colorism has affected her life. I think I would censor myself a little bit now. I never thought the play would get produced, so I was very free and vulnerable in a way.

Playwright Jocelyn Bioh. REUTERS/Brendan McDermid Why? When you're a playwright and your name starts to grow within the community, you start to have an awareness of the responsibility of your words. And I'm okay with having that responsibility because I know I'm doing something really different. I'm really blowing open how people see Black and African people on a theatrical stage. There's an incredible responsibility to that. The play takes place in Ghana, but these girls feel instantly recognizable. Did you know when you were writing it how universal they would be? I understood that there's a real rich universality we have, particularly in school and friendship dynamics. Those things are evergreen and universal. I knew what I was writing was different, (that) the girls and the people I was reflecting were different, but I didn't want to alienate audiences. That's part of why I added the subtitle. What's something we all know and recognize about the teenage experience? Mean girls. Paulina seems to believe that if she can just become Miss Ghana, she can escape the limits of her life. Is her obsession with beauty really an obsession with power and possibility? Probably. Ultimately, I think she really believes this is going to set her up for a successful life in entertainment. The play is set in 1986, and if you became Miss Ghana, Miss World, Miss Universe — any of those things — you could become a star. This is how we have Vanessa Williams or Halle Berry or Kenya Moore, if you're of the “Real Housewives” persuasion. (Another character,) Eloise, is a former Miss Ghana and did leave. She's come back now living a different life, (signifying that) in order to have success, you've got to get out. In order to have power, you have to get out. Maybe Paulina doesn't see the beauty and power that she can build in her own country. That's reflective of so many immigrant, particularly African immigrant, stories: In order to have success, you need to leave. I don't know if the play were set in 2026, (if) that would be the case now. I think the play would be very different. But for Paulina and her circumstances then, that is what she believed. The play deals so directly with colorism. Do you think colorism is in some ways more sensitive to talk about than racism? They're inextricably linked. The play largely talks about and shows the effects of colorism, but then ends with a global lesson on racism. And we've not moved on from it. When we started rehearsals for the play in August, the biggest news story was Lupita Nyong'o playing Helen of Troy in Christopher Nolan's film (“The Odyssey”). (Her casting) did not fit with whomever's standard of beauty (for) the woman whose face launched a thousand ships. Why didn't it fit? Why were there so many suggestions about, “Well, Zendaya's in the movie, why can't she play that part?” That's a very clear conversation about colorism, whether people are using that word or not.

When I wrote this play, it was really important for me to have that conversation because it had affected my life so much. Revisiting it now, especially in relation to these conversations that are happening globally, I'm like, well, we've not moved on from it. We can't move on from colorism because nobody's moved on from racism. I can't change people's minds. But if people come to see “School Girls” and their implicit bias can shift just a little bit, then I've done my job. The play is extremely funny until you realize how much pain is sitting underneath the humor. How deliberate is that? I really believe that comedy is just a funny way of being serious. Humor and pain are on two different sides of a truth coin. It's all rooted in truth. Paulina is a girl in the world who's trying to be affirmed and validated that she belongs there, that her beauty is widely accepted even if she knows that it's not. The lengths she goes to get there are what's comical, but it's rooted in something real that we all experience. At the end of the day, I'm a comedic writer and I want people to be entertained. But because I know the responsibility of who I'm introducing and the culture I'm introducing, I think there's a responsibility in also educating people. If I can make that medicine go down with a little bit of sugar, honey, agave, whatever you like, I'm willing to go there. The perspectives expressed in Culture Current are the subject’s own and do not necessarily reflect the views of Reuters News.

item.title: Isaias kills four, about 670,000 without power after landfall
item.description: The National Hurricane Center expects storm surges, flash flooding, damaging winds and a risk of tornadoes across parts of the US Southeast.
item.dc:creator: Rhea Abraham, Rajveer Pardesi, Marianna Parraga
item.content:encoded: Four people died after Hurricane Isaias made landfall early on Saturday, and about 670,000 residents in Florida, Alabama, Georgia and Mississippi were still without power as the storm weakened to a post-tropical cyclone, according to local authorities and electricity monitoring services. Two of the deaths resulted from trees falling on homes, according to local media and authorities. Authorities in Florida had received no search and rescue requests shortly after landfall in a sign of limited impact, Governor Ron DeSantis said. But hazardous conditions remained and storm surges, flash flooding, damaging winds and a risk of tornadoes across parts of the US Southeast were expected, the National Hurricane Center said. The tornado threat is expected to continue on Saturday across parts of the Florida Panhandle, Georgia and the Carolinas, the NHC said. In Florida, power restoration was marked as a priority, authorities said, while highways, bridges and airports were reopening, and teams were assessing the damage. "They're going to make assessments this morning, and I think that'll give us a good sense about the future for the rapidity of the power restoration," DeSantis told a press conference in Tallahassee. Some 16,000 utility linemen had prepared to respond to the storm, he said. About 420,000 customers in Florida, 190,000 in Alabama, 43,000 in Georgia and 17,000 in Mississippi had no power as of midday Saturday, according to tracking firm PowerOutage.us. A separate storm on the Pacific Ocean, Rachel, was moving toward the coast of northern Baja California on Saturday, bringing wind gusts and increased tides, which left another 7,000 people without power in California. Alabama's emergency management agency said the downed trees and power lines made travel hazardous in Houston County, which is under a flash flood warning. "Due to the impacts of Hurricane Isaias, all Houston County roads are closed until further notice," it posted on X. A category 2 hurricane when it hit Florida's coast and the first of the 2026 Atlantic season, Isaias is expected to produce gusty winds well inland before weakening below gale force later on Saturday, the NHC said. On Saturday, oil and gas producer Shell (SHEL.L) said it was beginning to redeploy personnel to its Mars, Olympus, Ursa, Vito and Appomattox assets in the Gulf, while Chevron (CVX.N) was advancing efforts to redeploy staff to its platforms and seeking to restore full production. "Remobilization of crews will continue through Sunday," it said. Despite the progress, about 69% of oil output and 57% of natural gas production in the US Gulf of Mexico remained shut on Saturday, slightly down from Friday numbers, the Marine Minerals Administration said. Some 113 production platforms representing 30% of the total remained evacuated, according to the agency. President Donald Trump, asked about hurricane preparations on Friday, told reporters outside the White House that it was "under control." The US Energy Department said on Saturday it authorized an emergency exchange of up to 4 million barrels of crude oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to address supply disruptions due to the hurricane. Emergency declarations were approved in Florida and Alabama to ensure federal resources would be available to respond to Isaias, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on X. "There's also a lot of hazards post-storm that people should be careful of, but so far, we've had a lot of assets in place that have not been called on," DeSantis told FOX News early on Saturday. In the coastal city of Pensacola, a lack of drinking water is a problem, the mayor said. Pensacola airport, Florida's 10th largest, was damaged by the storm and is closed to commercial flights until further notice.

item.title: India detains thousands, locks down Delhi to foil election chief protest
item.description: Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel deployed across the city, mobile internet services were suspended and dozens of metro stations and markets were shut as authorities moved to stop a rally organized by the Cockroach movement.
item.dc:creator: Saurabh Sharma, Sarita Singh, Sakshi Dayal
item.content:encoded: Police detained more than 2,000 protesters and the founder of the "Cockroach" youth movement in Delhi on Saturday as security forces [USN:L1N45V075 TEXT:"locked down"] parts of the capital to thwart a rally demanding the resignation of India's election chief. Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were deployed across the city, mobile internet services were suspended in the central business district and dozens of metro stations and markets were shut as authorities moved to stop a demonstration organised by the Cockroach movement. The protest was aimed at Chief Election Commissioner [USN:L4N45K0DB TEXT:"Gyanesh Kumar"] over a [USN:L1N45V037 TEXT:"revision of voter lists"] that critics say disproportionately benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). The movement had planned to gather thousands of people at Jantar Mantar in central Delhi, but the area was sealed off by security forces before the demonstration began. A home ministry official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told Reuters more than 2,000 people were detained in Delhi. Local media said about 400 protesters were held in India's financial hub, Mumbai. There was no immediate comment from police on the detentions. The United Nations human rights office expressed concerns over mass detentions before and during the protests. "We call on the authorities to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is fully respected and fulfilled," UN Human Rights Spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan said in a statement. He also urged authorities to engage in "meaningful dialogue" to address the "broadly held" concerns expressed. The Indian mission to the UN in Geneva, however, called the UN's concerns "misplaced" and said they constitute "an unwarranted interference in the internal affairs of India." It stressed that the right to peaceful assembly was guaranteed by India's Constitution. "As in every democracy, Indian citizens exercise this right subject to reasonable restrictions in the interest of public order," the statement added. MOVEMENT LEADERS HELD Police detained Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke and senior leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka when their flight from Mumbai landed in Delhi, the group said in a statement. Television footage showed Dipke challenging officers who approached him on board the aircraft. "I have come to be arrested, arrest me ... I am not afraid of you guys," he said. "No, this is not an arrest," one officer replied. "Please cooperate." The movement condemned what it called the "authoritarian detention" of its leaders, demanded their release and vowed to continue protesting. "We will continue our protest tomorrow, day after ... until Gyanesh Kumar resigns. We will be on the streets," CJP leader Ajinkya Shinde told reporters. CJP also said authorities refused to provide updates on the leaders' whereabouts or health, even after news arrived of the death of Dipke's grandmother. Police said Dipke was informed of her death and was offered help to return home for the funeral. Some opposition lawmakers and former chief ministers Mamata Banerjee of West Bengal, Arvind Kejriwal of Delhi, and Pinarayi Vijayan of Kerala were also detained, TV channels showed. Representatives of two digital news outlets said police briefly detained four of their reporters while they were covering the demonstrations. A Reuters journalist was also detained briefly before being released. Across the capital of about 20 million people, security forces set up checkpoints on major roads and entry points, boarded buses searching for protesters and inspected vehicles. Barricades and concrete blocks disrupted traffic while anti-riot vehicles equipped with tear-gas launchers guarded key routes. NEW CHALLENGE TO MODI The demonstrations represent one of the most serious tests yet for Modi, stemming from allegations that election authorities improperly revised voter rolls ahead of recent state polls. Protests intensified after the Indian Express reported last week that two election commissioners had questioned Kumar's voter-list revisions that removed roughly 130 million names from voter lists. Kumar has not commented but the Election Commission and the BJP have denied allegations of wrongdoing. The BJP says its electoral success reflects Modi's popularity and India's economic growth, and accuses opposition parties of spreading misinformation. The near [USN:L6N45U0IF TEXT:"daily protests"] come just months after demonstrations over exam paper leaks forced his [USN:L1N43R02E TEXT:"education minister to quit"]. The unrest also comes ahead of a series of important state elections beginning in early 2027. Rahul Gandhi, leader of the main opposition Congress party, said Modi's opponents would not back down. A senior BJP member, Ravi Shankar Prasad, said the party was not opposed to demonstrations but the street protests had been "weaponised" by rivals due to election defeats. DELETIONS AFFECTED STATE POLLS, OPPOSITION ALLEGES Opposition parties say the deletions affected the outcome of recent state elections won by the BJP and have cast a shadow over voting in the world's largest democracy. Election Commission data show about 130 million voter entries were removed during the verification exercise, including 63 million people who had relocated, 30 million who could not be traced and 28 million who had died. The commission says the removals relate to entries identified during the draft revision process and that any eligible voter incorrectly deleted can re-enrol.

item.title: Super Micro contractor pleads guilty in scheme to divert AI servers with Nvidia chips to China
item.description: Ting-Wei "Willy" Sun pleaded guilty to four counts.
item.dc:creator: Karen Freifeld, Jaspreet Singh
item.content:encoded: A contractor linked to Super Micro Computer (SMCI.O) has pleaded guilty in a scheme to illegally export computer servers containing advanced Nvidia (NVDA.O) AI chips to China, a federal court filing showed on Friday. Ting-Wei "Willy" Sun pleaded guilty to four counts, including conspiracies to violate US export controls, smuggle goods from the US, defraud the country and obstruct justice. He entered the plea on Thursday in U.S. District Court in Manhattan. The United States and China are competing for dominance in AI, with both investing billions of dollars in a technology seen as critical to economic growth, national security and military capabilities. In March, [USN:L1N4071M5 TEXT:"prosecutors charged"] Sun and two others associated with Super Micro, including a co-founder of the AI-server maker, with conspiring to divert about $2.5 billion worth of US AI technology to China in violation of export laws. The scheme began around October 2023, with Sun and others conspiring to export servers from a US manufacturer, widely believed to be Super Micro, to China without the required licenses, according to the indictment. Asked for comment on the guilty plea, California-based Super Micro referred to its prior statements that the company was not named as a defendant in the indictment and that it had no impact on its business operations. [USN:L4N40Q1GS TEXT:"Super Micro"] terminated Sun and cut ties with the other defendants earlier this year. A lawyer for Sun declined to comment. Also indicted were the co-founder Yih-Shyan "Wally" Liaw and Ruei-Tsang "Steven" Chang, who was a sales manager at Super Micro's Taiwan office, while Sun was a contractor. A lawyer for Liaw - who co-founded Super Micro in 1993 and joined its board in 2023 - did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Chang's lawyer could not immediately be reached for comment. The indictment described Sun as a broker and “fixer” who facilitated orders and took steps to conceal the scheme. He helped stage "dummy" servers in December 2025 and made false statements to a US Department of Commerce officer during an inspection of supposedly stored servers, which had already been diverted to China, according to the indictment. Washington has restricted sales of advanced AI chips to China, citing national security concerns. The indictment said Nvidia's B200, H100 and H200 graphics processing units, and servers containing them, were subject to the restrictions.

item.title: US lifts sanctions on daughter of Myanmar military-linked businessman
item.description: The United States lifted on Friday sanctions on the daughter of a Myanmar businessman accused of supporting the country's military, according to the US Treasury Department's website, after she filed a suit seeking removal from the blacklist.
item.dc:creator: Simon Lewis
item.content:encoded: The United States lifted on Friday sanctions on the daughter of a Myanmar businessman accused of supporting the country's military, according to the US Treasury Department's website, after she filed a suit seeking removal from the blacklist. The move comes after Reuters reported this week that the Trump administration had [USN:L6N45T16N TEXT:"opened talks with Myanmar's military-installed government"], reversing US policy that sought to isolate the generals who overthrew elected leaders in 2021. A State Department spokesperson said the decision to remove Myanmar national Theint Win Htet from the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List (SDN List) "reflects the administration’s determination that this designation no longer effectively supports US policy objectives related to Burma." "The administration is using a range of tools to advance key priorities regarding Burma, such as combating scam centers, improving Burma's domestic operating environment for US businesses, and encouraging a peace process to address the ongoing violence and humanitarian crisis," the spokesperson said, using the country's previous name. After the 2021 coup, former President Joe Biden's administration imposed sanctions on senior Myanmar military officers and companies it accused of providing support for the military junta, which triggered a nationwide civil war that has killed an estimated 100,000 people and displaced more than 3.5 million. The Treasury in January 2024 [USN:S0N3D107F TEXT:"targeted the "][USN:S0N3D107F TEXT:"Shwe Byain Phyu Group of Companies"], its founder Thein Win Zaw and his family, saying the company imported and distributed petroleum on behalf of the military and that the family owned at least 20 companies closely associated with the regime. Thein Win Zaw's adult daughter, Theint Win Htet, sued the Biden administration seeking her removal from the SDN List, but her case was dismissed in February 2025. The sanctions freeze any US assets of those targeted and generally bar Americans from dealing with them. The US in July 2025 [USN:L1N3TM01T TEXT:"lifted sanctions"] on several other Myanmar nationals and a firm under sanctions for aiding the military. Theint Win Htet filed a new complaint in July this year, arguing that she has no active role in her father's business affairs, adding that the sanctions had interrupted her studies in the US, where she completed a bachelor's degree at New York University and was enrolled in a master's program at Columbia University. "Plaintiff’s US credit cards have been blocked, her foreign bank accounts have been restricted, closed, or refused, and she has been unable to complete her university studies in the United States," said the complaint by Theint Win Htet, who said in the complaint she now lives with her mother in Bangkok. Her mother was removed from the sanctions list last year. Campaign group Justice For Myanmar denounced the US move at a time when it said the Myanmar military was escalating attacks on civilians. "It is deplorable that the US government continues to delist Myanmar cronies and their family members that provide funding for the junta's terror," the group said. Theint Win Htet's lawyer, Washington-based sanctions specialist Erich Ferrari, filed a notice with the US District Court for the District of Columbia on Friday voluntarily dismissing the lawsuit after her delisting. Ferrari declined to comment.

item.title: Erik Prince's forces suffer battlefield loss in Congo, former UFC fighter among wounded, sources say
item.description: Popular former UFC fighter Tim Kennedy was among the wounded in an ambush that killed or wounded at least 20 people deployed by Vectus Global.
item.dc:creator: Jessica Donati
item.content:encoded: Blackwater founder Erik Prince's forces suffered a major battlefield loss in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo in mid-September when enemy forces ambushed them, killing and wounding at least 20 people, including a popular former UFC fighter, sources close to the government and his company said. The frontline clash shows how Prince, an ally and supporter of US President Donald Trump, has taken on an expanded role in Congo through his company Vectus Global. The company, which also operates in Haiti and other parts of Africa, provides consulting and security services and previously [USN:L6N3XA0X0 TEXT:"helped Congo’s army"] secure the city of Uvira in South Kivu against Rwanda-backed rebels who control swathes of the east. A veteran special operator reported on his podcast earlier this week that former US Green Beret and Ultimate Fighting Championship contestant Tim Kennedy was injured in Congo. The involvement of Prince's forces and the number of casualties have not previously been reported. The attack in South Kivu on September 17 left about 20 dead and wounded, two sources working with Congo's government said. The dead included at least seven Congolese and a former member of New Zealand's Special Forces, while the wounded included Kennedy and another foreign contractor, the sources said. A Vectus Global representative declined to comment. The company has not previously suffered casualties in Congo, a source with direct knowledge of the operation said. One of the sources who works for Congo's government said that Rwandan forces backing the M23 rebels may have surprised them by tracking a drone used for surveillance operations to their location. Spokespeople for the Congolese and Rwandan governments and for the M23 did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Kennedy, the former mixed martial arts fighter, survived the attack with three gunshot wounds to the leg, three sources said, and is being treated at the Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in the suburbs of Washington. Kennedy has a popular podcast channel and millions of followers on social media. Trump is a fan of UFC, [USN:L6N42N00Z TEXT:"hosting fights"] at the White House this year. The US State Department and Walter Reed declined to comment. Kennedy's parents did not respond to requests for comment. A Congolese security source, who said some 20 people were wounded and killed in the attack, added that villagers were likely among the casualties as well. Reuters spoke to at least 10 sources either with direct knowledge of the attack or briefed on the outcome. PRINCE TOOK EXPANDED ROLE IN CONGO'S CONFLICT Prince's initial mandate in Congo was to secure and improve revenue collection from the country's vast mineral reserves, which have been plundered for decades, fuelling relentless conflict in the east. But in January and early February, his forces deployed to Uvira after Washington helped broker a deal for Rwandan-backed rebels to withdraw from the strategic town. The size of Prince's forces in Congo is unclear. One of the sources with direct knowledge of the attack said the Vectus team was travelling between locations when the ambush took place and its sophistication suggested Rwandan forces were involved. "It reinforces the need for DRC sovereignty to be restored. It's an incredibly dangerous place right now," the source said. Two other sources said the ambush was carried out by the Rwandan military. Prince is the founder of now-defunct private military firm Blackwater, some of whose members were pardoned in 2020 for killing Iraqi civilians. The State Department has said it does not have any contracts with Prince in Congo, though US officials have said they plan to work [USN:L1N43O0RW TEXT:"more closely with Vectus Global"] in Haiti. The deal for Rwandan-backed rebels to withdraw from Uvira was part of [USN:L6N3XA0X0 TEXT:"wider agreements"] brokered by the Trump administration to try to end the conflict in eastern Congo. POPULAR PODCASTER Kennedy, a father of four, has posted his views on politics, culture, fitness and more on social media. He also runs a popular YouTube podcast in which he interviews UFC fighters, veterans, cultural disruptors and others. He has often posted about his family, including four young children. In late August, he posted about having "incredible conversations about what being a man means and what sacrifice really looks like" with his son. He did not disclose details about his upcoming trip to Congo. The United Nations and Western powers say Rwanda backs M23, even exercising command and control over the group. Rwanda denies this. Fighting in the decades-long conflict flared early last year, with M23 fighters making rapid gains in the east, which is rich in tantalum, gold, lithium and other minerals.

item.title: Anthropic discloses fake tip to police among new rogue AI incidents
item.description: It is the first known instance in which AI appears to have tried to communicate a bogus tip to authorities, despite instructions not to create accounts or submit anything destructive, while not explicitly barred from submitting forms.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: An Anthropic artificial intelligence model submitted a false homicide tip to a Philadelphia police website, among a string of incidents the AI company disclosed on Friday detailing Claude models' unsanctioned manipulation of some government websites. It is the first known instance in which a rogue AI appears to have tried to communicate a bogus tip to authorities, despite instructions not to create accounts or submit anything destructive, while not explicitly barred from submitting forms. The cases are the latest examples of rogue or undesired behavior by the AI models of tech companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI. They add fuel to national concerns about the fast-advancing technology amid reports of corporate network hacks by AI agents, and researchers' warnings of an eventual existential threat to humanity. Many of the cases Anthropic revealed involved websites run by federal, state and local agencies. Anthropic said it briefed the White House and notified all the agencies involved, but did not disclose who those parties were. "Super intelligence companies must immediately disclose incidents involving their models and follow with swift, decisive action to remedy any and all harm," FTC Director of Public Affairs Joe Gabriel Simonson said on X. This process was "not optional," he said, adding that the Super Intelligence Force would fulfill its responsibility. The FTC said Anthropic disclosed to the SI Force on Friday its late September discovery of incidents involving what the task force called "unauthorized and fraudulent use of government and other systems". TIP ATTRIBUTED TO AUTOMATED TEST PROCESS On Friday, Philadelphia police said Anthropic notified them of the spurious tip this week, and attributed the submissions to an automated testing process. "The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the city is unacceptable," they said. The July 18 tip purported to come from someone who might have information about the case, police added. "I may have information regarding this case," Anthropic's model wrote in its submission. "I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around (the street named on the page) during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant." The brackets featured in Anthropic's statement. Previous incidents have involved AI agents hacking into vulnerable systems or commandeering unsanctioned platforms to communicate with one another. In September, Anthropic rival OpenAI apologized for the hacking of an Australian health data portal by a rogue AI agent, the first known instance of an AI agent exploiting a government website. A BOGUS TIP In two cases described on Friday, Anthropic’s models obtained for free public data normally only available for a fee. Another instanced revealed an obscure flaw that allowed use of a public tool hosted by a university. Claude models were also able to bypass restrictions by using free services that shorten URLs. Philadelphia police said the tip "was flagged as spam and was never forwarded to the Real-Time Crime Center for investigative vetting or dissemination." Knowingly giving false reports to law enforcement authorities is a misdemeanor under Pennsylvania law, which specifies "a person", however. This includes "information relating to an offense or incident when he knows he has no information relating to such offense or incident." Police quoted Anthropic as telling them the test process was stopped after discovery of the incident. The false tip was submitted through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com concerning an unsolved homicide. Police said they had no evidence of unauthorized access to their systems or compromise of their data.

item.title: Moroccan king says migration cooperation model with Spain hit limit
item.description: King Mohammed VI said on Friday that Morocco's efforts to curb irregular migration had produced "concrete results," but that the current cooperation model with Spain had reached its limits amid recurring crises.
item.dc:creator: Ahmed Eljechtimi
item.content:encoded: King Mohammed VI said on Friday that Morocco's efforts to curb irregular migration had produced "concrete results," but that the current cooperation model with Spain had reached its limits amid recurring crises. At least 70,000 people [USN:S8N3VJ0CQ TEXT:"crossed"] from Morocco into the enclave of Ceuta in July. Most have returned but thousands, including minors, [USN:L8N45Q015 TEXT:"remained"]. Speaking at the parliament's opening, the king cited "obsolete" and "unrealistic" Spanish court decisions that hindered cooperation on migration. "They are regrettably impeding the repatriation of minors and of fake asylum seekers, while fueling the greed of criminal networks," he said. Since the Ceuta migration crisis, [USN:L1N45A0G3 TEXT:"Spanish opposition"] parties have blamed Pedro Sanchez's government and [USN:L1N4520W0 TEXT:"accused"] Rabat of facilitating the crossing. Morocco rejected the accusations, blaming the crossing on social media and misinterpretations of a court ruling that appeared to open a legal loophole for arrivals by sea. Morocco's partnership with Spain was a "sovereign choice" and "it will never be subject to any pressure, threat, or blackmail," the king said. He added that Morocco would propose a vision centred on shared development, economic competitiveness and regional stability to its partners. Relations between Morocco and Spain have improved since Spain backed Morocco's autonomy plan for Western Sahara in 2022. But bilateral ties have faced a [USN:L1N45N08Q TEXT:"test"] since the Ceuta migration crisis. The king [USN:S8N3SV012 TEXT:"appointed"] Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri as the country's first female prime minister, after her party finished on top in the September 23 election. He urged members of parliament to put young people at the heart of public policies.

item.title: Strong Panama quake shakes nation, but avoids major destruction
item.description: A magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck southern Panama on Friday, damaging buildings and sending thousands into the streets, but the country appeared to escape widespread destruction or deaths.
item.dc:creator: Elida Moreno, Dave Sherwood
item.content:encoded: A magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck southern Panama on Friday, damaging buildings and sending thousands into the streets, but the country appeared to escape widespread destruction or deaths. The US Geological Survey said the earthquake hit at a depth of 12.6 km (7.8 miles), with an epicenter in a sparsely populated area about 200 km (124 miles) from the capital, and that some casualties were possible. In the following hours, even as more than 40 aftershocks rattled the isthmus nation, the Panama Canal and Cobre Panama copper mine reported normal operations and the Tocumen International Airport lifted a suspension on flights. Office workers in the upscale business hub of downtown Panama City fretted about how to get home in the snarl of traffic, after the quake sent thousands into the streets. Juan Sanchez, a 37-year-old economy ministry employee, waited for a bus he said he doubted would arrive. "They evacuated all of these buildings. Everyone is outside. Now the problem is, how do we get home?" President Raul Mulino traveled to Penonome, a city about halfway between the epicenter and Panama City, where some buildings collapsed and a church was damaged. Despite the force of Friday's tremor, the country appeared to have been spared the [USN:L6N44903E TEXT:"destruction"] of other recent powerful quakes in the [USN:L6N42X19G TEXT:"region"], with no deaths or injuries immediately reported. Back-to-back quakes in Venezuela in June killed several thousand people, while a quake in Colombia in August killed more than 300. An exposure report by the USGS estimated about 43,000 Panamanians lived in areas with at least severe exposure to the quake. This compares to nearly 1.4 million in the area of the twin quakes in Venezuela and over 1.6 million in the quake-hit zone of western Colombia. PROLONGED VIBRATIONS Nestor Luque, director of Panama's geosciences institute, attributed the quake to the Azuero Sona Fault System that he said contained a massive buildup of pressure that is occasionally released. "The seismic signals have traveled throughout the national territory and that is why it could be felt everywhere." In Panama City, Luque said he counted 40 seconds of vibrations, though other areas may have felt even longer tremors. Sabina Rios, who was on the sixth floor of an old US military-era building in Panama City, said the shaking was unusually strong and prolonged. "The quake felt strong and lasted a long time, the longest I’ve felt in years,” Rios said. Victor Pinzon, a 48-year-old maintenance worker, told Reuters he had watched high-rise window cleaners ride out the shaking. “It’s a miracle they didn’t get killed,” he said. “They looked like they were swinging in a hammock.” Strong earthquakes are not common in Panama, and some elderly residents were in tears as they evacuated into the streets. “We’re scared. It’s just the two of us old folks here. The house has cracked, and we’re afraid it could fall on us,” said Ricardo Brown, 74, in Herrera province in southern Panama, where he said he saw a number of damaged homes. Omar Smith, who heads Panama's civil protection agency, told news outlet Telemetro Reporta that impacts had also been reported in Chitre, the capital of Herrera, and along the coast in Los Santos province. The USGS estimated economic losses could amount to 1% to 10% of Panama's gross domestic product, and electricity provider Naturgy reported power outages in six provinces. Panama was due to hold a national evacuation drill on Monday of next week to test the country's emergency response.

item.title: US immigration chiefs defend shooting of New York man, attack 'sanctuary' policies
item.description: US immigration officials defended federal agents on Friday who shot and wounded a New York City man in his car with a young child believed to be his son in the back seat and rebuked Mayor Zohran Mamdani for his condemnation of immigration agents.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Allen, Joseph Ax
item.content:encoded: US immigration officials defended federal agents on Friday who shot and wounded a New York City man in his car with a young child believed to be his son in the back seat and rebuked Mayor Zohran Mamdani for his condemnation of immigration agents. US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said at a press conference that officers did not know the child was in the car at the time they opened fire and accused the man, a Dominican who was the target of the operation, of endangering both officers and the child. The man, identified by officials as Oscar Belgal, refused to exit his car when approached by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers on Thursday afternoon in Marble Hill, Manhattan's northernmost neighborhood. Before Belgal, federal immigration officers had shot at least 21 people, killing 7 of them, across the US since President Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025 promising record-breaking deportations, an unusually high number for civil law enforcement operations. Marcos Charles, a senior ICE official, said at the press conference that Belgal accelerated his car and struck two ICE vehicles and appeared to be "going towards officers" when they began shooting. In other violent incidents, initial accounts from ICE or the Department of Homeland Security have repeatedly been contradicted by video and other evidence, sometimes in court, and Reuters was unable to verify Charles' account. Belgal suffered a superficial wound to his neck, Charles said. He is being held in a detention facility outside New York state. Belgal's 5-year-old son was in the back seat at the time, according to police. Belgal can be seen sitting by a car with his hands cuffed behind him and patches of what appear to be fresh blood on the tarmac in a three-minute body-worn camera video released by the New York Police Department on Friday, with several agents dressed in plain clothes standing around him. One is holding a rifle and wearing a fluorescent reflective vest. A crowd of angry onlookers gathered outside a corner store shouts at the agents from the sidewalk. Several city police officers pick up Belgal by his arms and legs, put him in their car and take him to a hospital. "Yo, put pressure, put pressure!" one of the police officers instructs his colleagues with Belgal in the back of the police car. Mullin said body-worn camera video from ICE agents would also be released. Belgal is a Dominican who is in the country illegally and had previously evaded an effort by ICE agents to apprehend him in September, according to US officials. He pleaded guilty last year to fourth-degree grand larceny for stealing something from another person, leading to a sentence of five years on probation, and is due in court in December on charges of criminal sale of a controlled substance, to which he pleaded not guilty, according to New York court records. Speaking to reporters late on Thursday at the scene of the shooting, Mamdani, noting he himself was an immigrant, condemned ICE as "rotten to the core" and said he had tried unsuccessfully to secure Belgal's release in phone calls with Trump and Mullin. Mamdani said the shooting is "further devastating confirmation of what we have long known, which is that ICE operates with impunity, that they sow chaos and terror across our country, that they have killed far more of our neighbors than they could ever have claimed to save." In response on Friday, Mullin attacked Mamdani and criticized New York's "sanctuary" policies, which restrict how much city agencies and police cooperate with immigration authorities unless a person has been convicted of violent or otherwise serious felonies. Trump says aggressive efforts to deport immigrants are necessary to protect the safety of native-born Americans. Public defenders at agencies that have represented Belgal in court also condemned the shooting. Legal Aid said in a statement the shooting amounted to "an urgent call to rein in ICE's use of force and hold federal immigration agents accountable," calling on city prosecutors to investigate the agents involved.

item.title: Merz 'outraged' that German former Chancellor Schroeder attended Putin's birthday
item.description: Gerhard Schroeder has faced criticism over his links to Russian businesses and Putin.
item.dc:creator: Emanuele Berro, Friederike Heine
item.content:encoded: Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz is "deeply outraged" by former Chancellor Gerhard Schroeder's [USN:L8N45U2DQ TEXT:"visit"] to Vladimir Putin's home to celebrate the Russian president's birthday this week, a German government spokesperson said on Friday. Schroeder, who served as chancellor from 1998 to 2005, has faced criticism in Germany and abroad over his links to Russian business and Putin, ties that have persisted despite Moscow's 2022 invasion of Ukraine and subsequent waves of Western sanctions. "Putin alone is responsible for the war in Ukraine. His orders are the cause of immeasurable suffering, civilian casualties, families being torn apart, dead and wounded," the spokesperson said. "The chancellor sees ... it as downright immoral for Mr. Schroeder to attend such a celebration." Putin turned 74 on Thursday. Schroeder, 82, and his wife, So-Yeon Schroeder-Kim, who sometimes handles his communications, did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment. The visit also drew criticism from within Schroeder's own Social Democratic Party (SPD). The party's co-leader Lars Klingbeil, who is also Germany's finance minister in Merz's conservative-led coalition, called it "completely unacceptable" in view of the suffering caused to Ukraine's people, according to the Sueddeutsche Zeitung daily. Schroeder has been appointed to several high-ranking positions in Russian companies in the last 20 years. Shortly after stepping down, he became chairman of the shareholders' committee of Nord Stream, the Gazprom-led Baltic Sea pipeline project he had championed while in office, and later held senior positions at Russian oil producer Rosneft. Earlier this year, Putin said Schroeder would be his preferred interlocutor for talks on new security arrangements for Europe, an idea immediately rejected by the European Union and Merz's government. Last week, Schroeder joined the supervisory board of Russian retailer Hyperglobus, a spin-off of Germany's Globus Holding which operates more than 20 supermarkets in Russia.

item.title: Paris jitters, oil battles and a Bolsonaro-fuelled Brazil rally: The financial week in five charts
item.description: Every Friday, Reuters Open Interest distills the financial week into five key charts, spotlighting the major trends, surprises and overlooked moves that defined the past five days.
item.dc:creator: Anna Szymanski
item.content:encoded: Every Friday, Reuters Open Interest (ROI) distills the financial week into five key charts, spotlighting the major trends, surprises and overlooked moves that defined the past five days. 1. FRENCH FRACTURE MIKE DOLAN, ROI Finance & Markets Columnist: A surge of market anxiety over France's budget deficits and upcoming elections has seen French government borrowing rates and risk premia versus Germany rise to levels not seen since the heat of the euro crisis in 2011. This has weighed on other euro sovereign spreads and banking stocks while also sending the euro to an [USN:L4N45T025 TEXT:"18-month low"] against the dollar. A euro crisis redux with France at its centre would be expected to elicit a major European Central Bank response to contain spillovers and insulate the single currency. But a looming leadership change at the top of the central bank could [USN:L6N45R0YE TEXT:"complicate that process"] and potentially raise the bar for action. 2. INFLECTION POINT? JAMIE MCGEEVER, ROI Markets Columnist: The big question in markets right now is whether we may be [USN:L6N45U02K TEXT:"at, or near, an inflection point"]. The spiking "term premium" is one example, as it threatens to slam both stocks and bonds. The term premium is the estimated level of extra compensation investors demand in return for buying long-dated Treasuries over short-term debt. What's pushing it higher remains an open question: growing doubts about Federal Reserve credibility, fears of US debt debasement, or something else entirely. But whatever the cause, the central concern is whether it keeps rising. If it does, that may signal some serious economic and market problems ahead. 3. LET THE BATTLE COMMENCE RON BOUSSO, ROI Energy Columnist: Middle East oil producers have launched a battle to [USN:L6N45T150 TEXT:"recapture market share"] lost during the Iran war. The scramble to recover lost customers is becoming a defining feature of the post-blockade market. Gulf producers, eager to replenish state coffers after more than seven months of disruption, are increasing exports while some producers, including Iraq and [USN:S8N45108K TEXT:"Saudi Arabia"], have [USN:L1N45N03W TEXT:"offered deep discounts"] to buyers willing to load cargoes inside the Gulf. But will this tussle for market share result in dramatically lower prices at the pump? Probably not as long as getting oil through Hormuz remains [USN:L6N45Q087 TEXT:"risky, unpredictable and expensive"]. 4. BOLSONARO BOOST JAMIE MCGEEVER, ROI Markets Columnist: That rumbling beneath emerging market investors' feet may be the first tremors of what could be a political earthquake in Brazil. Right-wing candidate Flavio Bolsonaro — son of former President [USN:S0N42U07U TEXT:"Jair Bolsonaro"], who in 2025 was convicted of plotting a coup to remain in power after losing the 2022 election — did much better than expected in the first round of voting in Sunday's presidential election. From a financial markets viewpoint, at least, the [USN:L1N45R09E TEXT:"verdict"] is clear: investors seem pleased with the potential turn to the right. The sizzling rally in Brazilian assets (.BVSP) and the real on Monday says it all. 5. SERIOUSNESS DEFICIT? ANNA SZYMANSKI, ROI Editor-in-Charge: Most US voters believe the Trump administration, Congress and AI companies are not taking AI risks seriously enough, [USN:L6N45S14D TEXT:"according to a new Reuters/Ipsos poll"]. AI risks have become a hot-button US political issue amid workers' fears about job security, local opposition to data centers and even warnings from AI labs that the technology could pose an existential threat to humanity. President Donald Trump has continued to double down on support for what he calls "Super Intelligence" and the data-center infrastructure it requires, arguing that the US cannot afford to fall behind China in this tech race. With the midterm elections approaching, that support could become a liability for Republican candidates in tight races. Opinions expressed are those of the authors.
