item.title: Hurricane Simon strengthens off Mexico's Pacific coast, threatens tourist region
item.description: The storm is churning toward a coastline dotted with beach resorts and fishing towns.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Becerril
item.content:encoded: Hurricane Simon is rapidly intensifying off Mexico's Pacific coast, packing sustained winds of 110 mph (177 kph) as it churns toward a stretch of coastline dotted with beach resorts and fishing towns, the US National Hurricane Center said on Friday. Simon, nearing Category 3 strength, is forecast to become a dangerous Category 4 by Saturday as it approaches Mexico's southwestern and west-central Pacific coast, one of the country's most popular tourist regions, the NHC said. "Simon could deliver the most significant hurricane impact to this stretch of the Mexican Pacific coast since Lidia in 2023, which damaged thousands of homes and devastated crops along the Jalisco coast," said Tyler Roys, a senior meteorologist at AccuWeather. Simon is expected to make landfall on Sunday between Manzanillo — Mexico’s largest port and the main gateway for trade with Asia — and Puerto Vallarta, a popular beach destination and home to nearly 300,000 residents. In Manzanillo, fishermen were hauling their boats off the beach and authorities were putting up black flags along the coast to signal the beach was closed. The Mexican Navy activated emergency response personnel in Colima and restricted maritime traffic along parts of the Pacific coast, closing ports to smaller vessels and barring larger vessels from operating in Michoacan. Simon was about 195 miles (315 km) south of Manzanillo in the afternoon and crawling northwest, according to the NHC. Forecasters warned that Simon could bring life-threatening flooding and mudslides, with isolated rainfall totals reaching 30 inches (762 mm) in parts of Michoacan, Colima, Jalisco and Nayarit. Mexican authorities warned that heavy rainfall was expected in the states of Guerrero, Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco. [USN:L8N45L0P6 TEXT:"Last week"], Hurricane Polo made landfall on the Baja California Peninsula as a Category 2 storm, toppling trees and utility poles, flooding streets and causing other property damage.

item.title: Ukraine hits second major tech site, expanding range of targets inside Russia
item.description: Ukraine is widening the scope of its attacks inside Russia.
item.dc:creator: Mark Trevelyan, Gleb Stolyarov
item.content:encoded: Ukraine struck and partly disabled a major data centre operated by Russian technology company Yandex on Friday in the second such action in successive days, widening the scope of its attacks inside Russia after Moscow hit data hubs in Ukraine . Yandex, which is heavily involved in Russia's AI development and is sometimes called Russia's Google, said its data centre in the Kaluga region southwest of Moscow had been struck by Ukrainian drones and partly put out of action. Ukrainian arms maker Firepoint said Kyiv had used its FP-1 one-way attack drones to mount the strike against what it called Yandex's biggest data centre and said that several of its modules had been completely knocked out of action. A day earlier, a Ukrainian attack [USN:L8N45U1P7 TEXT:"shut down Yandex's data hub in Sasovo"], southeast of Moscow, where two of the three supercomputers used to develop the company's AI model are housed. Yandex said it was facing a difficult challenge to maintain its services, used by millions of Russians daily for navigation, music, movies, food orders and other tasks. It also provides cloud computing services on which many businesses depend. YANDEX SHARES FALL ON RUSSIAN EXCHANGE Alexander Savitsky, who runs a start-up dating app called Pulse with 8,000 users, told Reuters that none of them had been able to access it since Thursday. He said the company was unable to reach its backup database in Yandex Cloud and was getting an "internal error" message when trying to restore it elsewhere. "We have no confirmation of actual data loss, but the situation is serious: the project represents three years of work," Savitsky said. "The main risk is losing users and their trust: people can't use the app, and there's no telling how many will return once service is restored." Yandex said it had struck a deal with other cloud providers to enable clients to swiftly move their data and services. Its shares fell by more than 4% on the Moscow exchange. "The risks involve not only the potential temporary unavailability of Yandex services and lost revenue in specific segments but also the company's extensive base of B2B clients," said Maryana Lazaricheva, head of equity research at T-Investments. She said the company could redistribute some of the load to its other data centres. "However, if the chain of attacks continues, this possibility vanishes, which could lead to even more severe consequences." BOTH SIDES EXPAND RANGE OF ECONOMIC TARGETS Locked in a deadly [USN:L1N45U0VZ TEXT:"war of attrition"] after more than four years of fighting, both Russia and Ukraine have expanded drone attacks this year on infrastructure targets, from energy facilities and refineries to ports and vessels carrying oil and grain, [USN:L1N44L05J TEXT:"e-commerce warehouses"] and, most recently, data centres. The full scale of the disruption caused by the attacks was not immediately clear, although messages appeared on at least one Yandex app warning of potential problems in its operation. Yandex said it was working around the clock to try to restore services which had been disrupted. "Right now this is our most important task, but unfortunately it is not an easy one," it said. Russia has struck Ukrainian data centres and telecommunications infrastructure over the past month, including targets in central Kyiv. "We always respond in mirror-like fashion," Ukrainian President [USN:L1N45U08A TEXT:"Volodymyr Zelenskiy"] said on Thursday. He confirmed on Friday that his drones had struck the Kaluga data centre in what he called "our tit-for-tat response". The regional governor said nine people had been injured in Ukraine's attacks, five of whom were being treated in hospital. SPARTAK MOSCOW AMONG WEBSITES CITING DIFFICULTIES Ukraine has previously targeted the warehouses of specific companies it deems central to Russia's economy, including dozens of sites operated by e-commerce giants Wildberries and Ozon. Russia responded by striking their Ukrainian equivalents. Yandex operates five data centres, two of which have already been hit. It said in 2021 that the Sasovo data hub, which was struck on Thursday, hosted two of its three supercomputers built around Nvidia A100 chips, which it uses to train its YandexGPT large AI model. Yandex has declined to say whether the supercomputers were affected by the attack. Multiple online services in Russia reported technical issues on Thursday, including real estate aggregator Cian, a book portal called Litmarket, and the websites of Russian Railways and professional football club Spartak Moscow. Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centres have forced some of them to suspend operations, while 100,000 households suffered temporary internet outages after one attack. Ukraine's digital minister told Reuters last month that the country was responding by moving digital infrastructure underground.

item.title: Central banks face test. Will they be good cops or bond villains?
item.description: A standoff between the banks and their governments may come as a bond-market crunch reopens questions about the political independence of the banks.
item.dc:creator: Mike Dolan
item.content:encoded: A standoff between central banks and their cash-strapped governments may well be looming as an intensifying [USN:L6N45U0LN TEXT:"bond market crunch"] reopens questions about the political independence of the banks well beyond their interest-rate policy. Central banks currently appear reluctant to rebuild holdings of sovereign debt, yet those holdings played a significant role in the swelling public borrowing over the past decade. Moving forward, that means either an improbable fiscal tightening will need to emerge or political knives will be sharpened. Numerous elections in the US, France, Italy and Spain over the coming year mean significant spending cuts are unlikely to be on the agenda. If bond markets continue to tighten — as we've seen in recent weeks — political pressure on central banks to steady the ship will rise even further. Seeing the problem coming like a slow-motion car crash, central banks are trying to nuance their position. On one hand, a post-pandemic consensus has built around further "normalization" of their bond-packed balance sheets. This includes a retrospective disdain for using bond accumulation as a monetary policy tool. On the other hand, policymakers want to keep all options open for temporary fixes in the event of market malfunctioning or another left-field shock. Bank for International Settlements (BIS) boss Pablo Hernandez de Cos this week laid out some principles for using emergency tools if conditions get rough, using the example of the Bank of England's (BoE) limited and brief support for stressed British gilts during the budget blow-up in 2022. "A key challenge is to bolster market confidence without overstimulating the economy in the longer term," he said of such emergency tools. "Central banks should try to better distinguish programmes for market functioning from those for monetary stimulus." But the problem with a middle-ground, [USN:L6N45T16X TEXT:"only-in-emergencies"] approach is that sometimes debt markets can get squeezed even when there isn't an acute crisis. Just look at the current global bond selloff. Markets are not necessarily malfunctioning, and despite the clear energy hit from the Iran war , there's no global shock on the scale of COVID-19 or the 2008 banking crash to justify a red alert. Yet markets continue to inflict maximum pain on government debt-service bills. Should this continue, alongside a relatively hot AI-infused economy and above-target inflation rates, monetary policymakers could find themselves in a very tough spot. If central banks do step in, the lines between "backstops," monetary policy and direct government support could become blurred, and central bankers could once again find themselves criticised for enabling rising government debt loads. Yet governments across the developed world may expect them to do just that if sovereign bond yields keep increasing. Rising debt-service bills are coming at a time when ageing demographics in most Group of Seven (G7) economies have already been heaping pressure on pension and healthcare systems, while defence spending is set to spiral higher amid increasingly fraught geopolitics. Pointing to forecasts that global government debt will exceed annual global GDP by 2030, [USN:L1N45S0Z3 TEXT:"International Monetary Fund head Kristalina Georgieva"] this week warned rich governments to deliver credible fiscal-consolidation plans urgently and not fall back on central banks to bail them out. "I would call this 'monetary cowboys', running to the rescue of the fiscal agents, and my message is: please don't." HOW DID WE GET HERE? For context, we need to rewind a bit. Of the multiple reasons cited for the intense government bond market selloff in recent months, a big question revolves around the gaping hole left in debt markets by the gradual withdrawal of G7 central banks from the swelling debt piles they facilitated following 2008. The selloff has pushed long-term US sovereign borrowing costs to their highest in almost a quarter of a century. Perhaps the best way to understand how artificially cheap borrowing distorted the picture is to examine how quickly governments accumulated debt when their central banks were buying bonds and effectively underwriting large chunks of it. The Washington-based Institute of International Finance recently estimated that even though average government borrowing costs across the G7 are back at mid-2008 levels, annual interest expenses are 85% higher because G7 government debts have almost trebled to more than $60 trillion in the interim. Advanced economies collectively are now paying over $3.3 trillion to service bonds alone, it said, which is more than their estimated spending on either AI, defence or clean energy. But coinciding with, and aggravating, the recent surge in government debt costs has been the steady pruning of central bank balance sheets over the past four years. The aggregate G7 central bank balance sheet peaked at over $30 trillion of bonds in early 2022 and has been cut by about a third since then.Along with the sharp rise in central bank policy rates to choke off inflation, that one-third reduction has coincided with a 40% drop in long-term G7 government bond indexes and a four-percentage-point spike in their implied borrowing rate. Have central banks exited too much or too quickly, and should they pause that withdrawal until they rethink it? BALANCE SHEET PHILOSOPHY Opinion on the wisdom of so-called quantitative easing (QE) — massive central-bank bond-buying programs — has done an almost 180-degree turn since the inflation spikes and debt explosions of the pandemic and its aftermath. For many, the banking crash of 2008 and 2020's COVID-19 lockdowns justified extraordinary one-off balance sheet reactions from the Federal Reserve and others. But many also now criticize the continuous use of bond buying as an ongoing monetary tool, arguing that it underwrote the massive expansion of government debt over the past 20 years. Much of the central bank world now feels the experiment may have been misguided at best, both because it tiptoed into quasi-fiscal territory and because of a variety of market distortions and inequality questions that arose from what was essentially direct support for wealthier asset owners. New Fed Chair and long-time balance-sheet-expansion sceptic [USN:S8N40E0AX TEXT:"Kevin Warsh "]claims the whole 18-year QE episode "borders on fiscal policy." He has already set up one of his Fed reform task forces to look at ways to reduce the balance sheet holdings further. On the other side of the pond, the [USN:L8N4590WV TEXT:"BoE"] is still actively selling gilts, albeit with recent plans to concentrate sales in short-dated paper. And the European Central Bank is still actively running down its balance sheet, which amounts to more than 40% of euro zone GDP, even as the region faces echoes of the 2011-12 euro debt crisis in French bond markets. A change of [USN:L6N45R0YE TEXT:"ECB leadership"] is also on the horizon, and the leading candidates don't appear to have an appetite for a return to the 2010s and the firefighting activism of former chief Mario Draghi. TWITCHIER TREASURIES There is also the question of who is holding government debt. The reduction of G7 central bank bond holdings has coincided with reduced pension-fund demand for long-dated government debt as defined-benefit schemes dwindle and pension savers retire. Those gaps left by long-term investors keen on safety and steady coupons have increasingly been filled by more speculative, short-term players such as hedge funds, who are much more sensitive to big price shifts, vulnerable to short-term interest rate changes and prone to herding in volatile conditions. Hedge fund activity in sovereign bond markets has been the focus of regulators for years. While everyone welcomes the demand and liquidity they provide, there is now growing concern about the flipside of that if this "fast money" base gets twitchy. Some efforts have been made to reduce [USN:L6N45R0WM TEXT:"excessive leverage"] in government bond markets, but no matter how that pans out, the scale of [USN:L6N44U0ZU TEXT:"hedge fund activity"] in these markets, and by extension the exposure of the banks and trading houses that provide them with leverage, makes for a more skittish environment. "These buyers are more inclined to sell bonds in response to higher short-term interest rates — funding leg sensitivity — and charge a higher price for the risk of further upward moves," wrote Carlyle strategist Jason Thomas. "When coupled with the growth in the outstanding volume of debt, this new class of investors has left bond markets more fragile and sensitized to front-end repricing." This sensitivity helps to explain the recent disturbance in Treasury markets, which seems to have been driven largely by the Fed changing course on short-term rates. SMBC Nikko's rates strategist Joseph Abate cites Fed studies trying to quantify that sensitivity. Fed economist Phillip Monin estimates that hedge fund demand for [USN:L1N45E0NO TEXT:"cash-futures arbitrage plays "]has increased fourfold since 2020 and is now 3.5% of outstanding Treasury supply. Another Fed study last month by Daniel Beltran and Canlin Li found that the market's sensitivity to new supply had doubled over the past decade, with every 1% increase in new debt, some $300 billion or more, increasing 5-year yields by 8 basis points. Regulators, governments and central banks are watching this closely. But any planned tightening of rules could well have adverse effects at a politically risky moment. While the answer, in theory, may be reducing the supply of government debt, in practice, that is very unlikely to occur. The alternative solution lands back in the lap of now more hesitant central banks — kicking and screaming perhaps. (The opinions expressed here are those of Mike Dolan , a columnist for Reuters.) item.content:encoded: Ukraine-Une attaque russe fait 20 morts à Zaporijjia, passe d'armes Zelensky-Trump ZAPORIJJIA, Ukraine, 10 octobre(Reuters) - Vingt personnes, dont trois enfants, ont été tuées samedi lors d'une attaque russe contre la ville de Zaporijjia, dans le sud de l'Ukraine, au lendemain de l'annonce par le président américain Donald Trump d'un accord levant les sanctions sur le diesel russe, un revers majeur pour Kyiv. USA-La survivante d'une tentative d'exécution quitte l'hôpital et retourne en prison 10 octobre (Reuters) - Christa Pike, la condamnée à mort dont l'exécution a échoué la semaine dernière dans le Tennessee, est sortie samedi de l'hôpital pour être renvoyée en prison où elle continuera de recevoir des soins médicaux, ont indiqué ses avocats. L'Érythrée demande à l'Onu d'intervenir dans son conflit avec l'Éthiopie 10 octobre (Reuters) - L'Érythrée a demandé samedi au Conseil de sécurité de l'Onu de prendre des mesures dissuasives à l'encontre de l'Éthiopie, selon une lettre consultée par Reuters, faisant valoir que les accusations d'incursion formulées par Addis-Abeba à son encontre équivalaient à une "déclaration de guerre". Léon XIV condamne la peine de mort, alors que Trump envisage de diffuser une exécution en direct ROME, 10 octobre (Reuters) - Le pape Léon XIV a réitéré samedi sa condamnation de la peine de mort, soulignant qu'elle portait atteinte au caractère sacré de la vie humaine et privait les personnes de toute chance de rédemption, quelques jours après que le Pentagone a annoncé son intention de diffuser une exécution en direct. Report à 2027 des élections palestiniennes RAMALLAH, Cisjordanie occupée, 10 octobre (Reuters) - Le président palestinien Mahmoud Abbas a annulé samedi les élections législatives prévues en novembre en raison de la dégradation de la situation dans les territoires palestiniens et fixé au 11 septembre 2027 la tenue simultanée des élections présidentielle et législatives, a rapporté l'agence de presse officielle palestinienne WAFA. Trump estime que la Norvège porte une "tache indélébile" pour ne pas lui avoir décerné le prix Nobel de la paix SYRACUSE, New York, 9 octobre (Reuters) - Le président américain Donald Trump s'est plaint amèrement vendredi de ne pas avoir reçu le prix Nobel de la paix, estimant que cette décision avait jeté une tache sur la Norvège. L'ouragan Isaias s'affaiblit après avoir touché terre en Floride 9 octobre (Reuters) - L'ouragan Isaias s'est rapidement affaibli vendredi après avoir touché terre près de Destin, en Floride, a fait savoir vendredi le Centre américain des ouragans (NHC). Ukraine-Poutine minimise une reprise immédiate des discussions, dit le Kremlin MOSCOU, 10 octobre (Reuters) - Le président russe Vladimir Poutine a dit vendredi à son homologue américain Donald Trump que Kyiv avait sapé la possibilité d'une reprise immédiate des négociations de paix trilatérales après avoir mené des frappes de drones à Moscou durant les élections législatives qui se sont déroulées le mois dernier, a fait savoir le Kremlin. Trump annonce un accord avec Poutine sur la livraison de diesel WASHINGTON, 9 octobre (Reuters) - Le président américain Donald Trump a annoncé vendredi qu'à l'issue d'une discussion "très fructueuse" qu'il avait eue avec Vladimir Poutine, la Russie avait accepté de livrer immédiatement plus de 300.000 tonnes de diesel sur les marchés américain et mondial. Le copilote de Flydubai voulait s'inspirer du 11-Septembre - procureur Le copilote omanais du vol Flydubai à destination d'Israël dérouté le 30 septembre vers l'Arabie saoudite voulait s'emparer des commandes de l'avion et le précipiter sur l'aéroport de Tel Aviv-Ben Gourion, a déclaré vendredi le procureur général des Emirats arabes unis, cité par l'agence officielle émiratie.

Bientôt, elle sera seule à bord. Cyclisme-Seixas remporte le Tour de Lombardie, son premier monument 10 octobre (Reuters) - Paul Seixas (Decathlon-CMA CGM) a remporté samedi le Tour de Lombardie, le premier monument du cyclisme de sa jeune carrière. Basket-Wembanyama soutient les manifestations lycéennes La star du basket français Victor Wembanyama a apporté jeudi soir son soutien aux lycéens et étudiants qui manifestent depuis plusieurs semaines pour exiger de meilleures conditions d'enseignement. Football: Ceferin finalement candidat à sa réélection à la tête de l'UEFA Le président de l'UEFA Aleksander Ceferin a annoncé jeudi qu'il était finalement candidat à sa réélection à la tête de l'instance européenne. Football: Infantino réaffirme le soutien de la Fifa au football africain Le président de la Fifa, Gianni Infantino, a promis jeudi davantage de moyens pour l'Afrique lors d'une conférence au Cap-Vert dans l'un de ses rares discours publics depuis son projet avorté de céder une partie des droits commerciaux des compétitions de la Fifa à des investisseurs privés. Rallye: Les organisateurs du Dakar envisagent un autre parcours en Arabie saoudite Les organisateurs du Dakar travaillent sur un parcours alternatif pour que la 49e édition, prévue en janvier, puisse se tenir en Arabie saoudite malgré la situation au Moyen-Orient, ont indiqué à Reuters trois sources impliquées dans le championnat du monde de rallye-raid . Basket: La NBA et la Fiba réaffirment leur volonté de lancer une ligue européenne La NBA et la Fédération internationale de basket (Fiba) ont réaffirmé jeudi leur intention de créer une ligue en Europe, deux jours après le rejet par l'Euroligue d'une proposition de collaboration formulée par son homologue nord-américaine, qui souhaite lancer son projet NBA Europe à l'automne 2027. Football: Arsenal prolonge son entraîneur Mikel Arteta jusqu'en 2030 Arsenal a annoncé mercredi la prolongation de contrat de son entraîneur Mikel Arteta jusqu'en 2030 après une saison remarquable lors de laquelle il a mené le club londonien au titre de Premier League et en finale de la Ligue des champions. Football-Messi fait ses adieux à l'équipe d'Argentine Lionel Messi a signé mardi une dernière prestation de grande classe, marquant un but et délivrant deux passes décisives à l'occasion de son ultime match sous le maillot de l'équipe d'Argentine remporté face au Bénin (3-0), en amical, après une carrière internationale de 21 ans. Football: La Fédération norvégienne saisit deux commissions de la Fifa sur la gouvernance et l'éthique La Fédération norvégienne de football (NFF) a annoncé mardi avoir déposé deux requêtes parallèles auprès de deux commissions de la Fifa concernant trois récents dossiers qui ont suscité la controverse dans le football mondial.
